quote: Wie viele Substi- tutionen geben zusammengesetzt die identische?
english: How many substitutions, when composed, give the identity?
topic: Hilbert finishes a remark on the correct criterion for a definition, then plans to extend the principle of continued identities to permutation groups and to Kummer's theory of ideal numbers, and begins a remark comparing mathematicians to miners.

triage.modern_statement: The note is too short to pin down one meaning. Read literally, it asks how many k-tuples (σ1,…,σk) of permutations in S_n (or in some permutation group G) have product σ1σ2…σk equal to the identity. With no further conditions the answer is trivial: |G|^(k-1), because the first k-1 factors can be anything and the last one is then fixed. The question only becomes a real research question with an extra condition. One version fixes the conjugacy classes, i.e. the cycle types, of the factors. Another sets all factors equal, so it asks how many solutions x^n = 1 has in G. A third asks how often one substitution must be composed with itself to give the identity, which is its order (for a permutation, the lcm of its cycle lengths). Which of these Hilbert meant, if any, cannot be told from the note. The surrounding plan to apply 'continued identities' to permutation groups suggests he was thinking about relations among substitutions.
triage.answered_by: No specific later answer to this note can be identified. The nearest well-known results were in fact obtained, mainly by F. G. Frobenius in the 1890s. In 1895 he proved that if n divides |G|, the number of solutions of x^n = 1 in G is a multiple of n. He also gave a character-theoretic formula for the number of solutions of product equations such as [x1,y1]…[xk,yk] = g. This is now standard theory (character formulas for counting solutions of equations in finite groups). The related Frobenius conjecture was later settled using the classification of finite simple groups. The note is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Frobenius's theorem: if n divides the order of a finite group G, the number of solutions of x^n = 1 in G is a multiple of n.
Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry on the Frobenius conjecture, which grew out of this counting theorem.
Frobenius gave a character formula for the number of solutions in G^(2k) of [x1,y1]…[xk,yk] = g.
Characters are still used to count solutions of equations in finite groups, e.g. divisibility results by Solomon and others.

triage.why: The note is one short question, left open on the page, written in a planning context. It can be read several ways: the trivial count of tuples, counts with given cycle types (Frobenius character theory), the solutions of x^n = 1 (Frobenius 1895), or the order of a permutation. Every reading is either trivial or was answered by classical 1890s group theory, mainly Frobenius. However, no source ties Hilbert's note to any of these results, and I found no published discussion of this diary entry. Counting solutions of equations in groups with characters is still being researched, but whether that bears on Hilbert's note depends on which reading is right.
